translations.text: Jesus went away across the sea of Galilee, and so on.
"The Saviour went across the Sea of Galilee, which is called Tiberias, and a great multitude followed him, because they had seen the signs that he worked on the sick.
Then the Saviour went up onto a hill and sat there with his disciples, and the holy Eastertide was then very near.
Then the Saviour looked up and saw that a great crowd was coming toward him, and he said to one of his disciples, who was called Philip, 'With what can we buy bread for these people?'
He said this to test the disciple; he himself knew what he would do.
Then Philip answered, 'Even if two hundred pennies' worth of bread were bought here, each of them could not get even one bite of it.'
Then one of his disciples, who was called Andrew, Peter's brother, said, 'Here a boy is carrying five barley loaves and two fishes, but what use is that for so great a crowd?'
Then the Saviour said, 'Make the people sit down.' And there was much grass in that place, pleasant to sit on. And they all sat down, about five thousand men.
Then the Saviour took the five loaves, and blessed them, and broke them, and distributed them among those who were sitting; in the same way he also distributed the fishes; and they all had enough.
When they were all full, the Saviour said to his disciples, 'Gather up the leftovers, so that they are not lost.'
And they gathered up the fragments, and filled twelve baskets with the leftovers.
The people, when they saw this sign, said that Christ was the true prophet who was to come into this world."
The sea which the Saviour crossed signifies this present world, to which Christ came and which he passed through; that is, he came to this world in human nature, and passed through this life;
he came to death, and rose from death; and he went up onto a mountain and sat there with his disciples, because he ascended to heaven, and now sits there with his saints.
The sea is rightly compared to this world, because at times it is calm and pleasant to row on, and at times also very rough and fearful to be on.
So is this world: at times it is prosperous and pleasant to live in, and at times it is also very harsh and mingled with various things, so that very often it is most unpleasant to dwell in.
Sometimes we are healthy, sometimes sick; now happy, and then again in great unhappiness; therefore this life, as we said before, is compared to the sea.
When the Saviour had sat down up on the mountain, he lifted up his eyes and saw that a great crowd was coming toward him.
All those who come to him, that is, those who turn to the true faith, the Saviour sees, and on them he has mercy,
and he enlightens their minds with his grace, so that they may come to him without error, and to them he gives spiritual food, so that they do not grow faint on the way.
When he asked Philip where they could buy bread for the people, he revealed Philip's ignorance.
Christ knew well what he would do, and he knew that Philip did not know it. Then Andrew said that a boy there was carrying five barley loaves and two fishes.
Then the Saviour said, "Make the people sit down," and so on, as we told you before.
The Saviour saw the hungry people, and he mercifully fed them, both through his goodness and through his might.
What could goodness alone do, unless there were power along with the goodness? His disciples also wanted to feed the people, but they had nothing to do it with.
The Saviour had the good will to feed them, and the power to carry it out.
God has worked many wonders, and works them daily; but those wonders have become greatly cheapened in men's sight, because they are so very customary.
It is a greater wonder that God Almighty feeds the whole world every day and guides the good, than was that wonder when he filled five thousand men with five loaves:
but men marvelled at that, not because it was a greater wonder, but because it was unusual.
Who now gives fruit to our fields, and multiplies the harvest from a few grains, but he who multiplied the five loaves?
The power was then in Christ's hands, and the five loaves were as if they were seed, not sown in the earth, but multiplied by him who made the earth.
This miracle is very great, and deep in its meanings. Often someone sees fair letters written, and then he praises the writer and the letters, and does not know what they mean.
He who has knowledge of the letters praises their fairness, and reads the letters, and understands what they mean. We look at a picture in one way, and at letters in another way.
Nothing more is needed for a picture than that you see it and praise it; it is not enough that you look at letters, unless you also read them and understand the meaning.
So it is also with the miracle that God worked with the five loaves: it is not enough that we wonder at the sign, or praise God for it, unless we also understand the spiritual meaning.
The five loaves that the boy carried signify the five books which Moses the leader set down in the old law. The boy who carried them, and did not taste of them, was the Jewish people,

who read the five books and knew no spiritual meaning in them, until Christ came and opened the books, and revealed their spiritual meaning to his disciples, and they afterwards to all Christian people.

We cannot now expound all the five books, but we tell you that God himself composed them, and Moses wrote them, for the guidance and teaching of the old people of Israel, and also for us in a spiritual sense.
Those books were written about Christ, but the spiritual meaning was hidden from the people until Christ himself came to men and opened the secret of the books according to the spiritual sense.

The other evangelists relate that the Lord distributed the loaves and fishes to the disciples, and the disciples served them to the crowds. He broke the five loaves and gave them to his disciples, and commanded them to carry them to the people;
because he taught them the spiritual doctrine, and they went throughout the whole world and preached, just as Christ himself had taught them.
As he broke the loaves, they were multiplied and grew in his hands;
For the five books were spiritually examined, and wise teachers expounded them and composed many other books from those books; and with the teaching of those books we are spiritually fed every day.
The loaves were of barley. Barley is very hard to prepare, and yet it feeds a man when it is ready.
So the old law was very hard and obscure to understand; but nevertheless, when we come to the fine meal, that is, to its meaning, then it feeds our mind and strengthens it with the hidden teaching.
There were five loaves, and five thousand men were fed there; because the Jewish people were subject to God's law, which stood written in five books.

When Christ asked Philip, and tested him, as we read before, he signified by that question the ignorance of the people who were under the law and did not know the spiritual meaning that was hidden in the law.
The two fishes signified the psalm-singing and the sayings of the prophets. One of them made known and proclaimed Christ's coming with psalm-singing, and the other with prophecy.
Now the two writings, that is, psalmody and prophecy, are as it were a relish to the five barley loaves, that is, to the five books of the law.
The people who feasted there sat up on the grass. The grass signified fleshly desire, just as the prophet said,
"All flesh is grass, and the glory of the flesh is like the blossom of plants."

Now everyone who wishes to sit at God's feast and partake of the spiritual teaching must tread down the grass and sit upon it; that is, he must subdue the carnal lusts and always bend his body to God's service.
Five thousand men were counted at that feast, because the people who belong to the spiritual feast must be made manly, just as the apostle said; he said,
"Be watchful, and stand firm in the faith, and act manfully, and be strengthened in heart."
But if a woman is made manly, and strong for God's will, she is then counted among the men who sit at God's table.
The number thousand is perfect, and no number rises above it. By that number is signified the perfection of the people who feed their souls with God's teaching.
"The Saviour then commanded them to gather up the leftovers, so that they should not be lost; and they filled twelve baskets with the fragments."
The leftovers of the meal, that is, the depths of the teaching which worldly men cannot understand, the teachers must gather up so that they are not lost, and keep them in their vessels,
that is, in their hearts, and always have it ready, to bring forth the wisdom and the teaching both of the old law and of the new. They then gathered twelve baskets full of the fragments.
That twelvefold number signified the twelve apostles, because they received the hidden mysteries of the teaching, which the unlearned people could not understand.
"The people who saw that miracle said of Christ that he was the true prophet who was to come."
They spoke truly, in some respects: he was a prophet, because he knew all things to come, and also prophesied many things which will be fulfilled without doubt.
He is a prophet, and he is the prophecy of all prophets, because all the prophets prophesied about him, and Christ fulfilled all their prophecies.
The people then saw that miracle, and they marvelled greatly at it. That miracle is written down, and we have heard it.
What their eyes did for them, our faith does in us. They saw it, and we who did not see it believe it;
and we are therefore counted better, just as the Saviour said of us in another place, "Blessed are those who do not see me, and yet believe in me, and glorify my wonders."
The people then said of Christ that he was a true prophet.
Now we say of Christ that he is the Son of the Living God, who was to come to redeem all the world from the power of the devil and from the torment of hell.
The people did not know enough good to say that he was God, but they said that he was a prophet.
We now say, with full faith, that Christ is a true prophet, and the Prophet of all prophets, and that he is truly the Son of Almighty God,
as mighty as his Father, with whom he lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, ever without end in eternity. Amen.
